frase_gancho.texto: A split face: half life, half skull.

puente_narrativo.texto: From death we move on to the life that defies it. The “pretty ladies” in the next display case show off their hairstyles, adornments, and hips of fertile earth.

guion_corto.texto: It fits in the palm of your hand, yet it holds an enormous idea. This little clay face from Tlatilco measures about eight centimeters and is split down the middle. On one side, a living face, with a full cheek, an open eye, and a shaped mouth. On the other, a skull, with a hollow eye socket and bared teeth. It is not a sad or macabre face: it is an idea. Life and death are not enemies, but two faces of the same thing. For the people of this village, the seed must be buried in order to be born, and the sun must descend into darkness in order to rise again. It is more than three thousand years old and is one of the oldest expressions of Mesoamerican duality.

guion_largo.texto:
Do you remember the [Tamayo mural](mna_s00_mural_tamayo), with the serpent and the jaguar at the entrance? The idea that the world is held together by pairs of opposites that need each other is very old. Long before the Mexica and their god of duality, Ometéotl, the people of Tlatilco were already shaping it in clay. This little face is one of the earliest proofs.

First, look at the line that splits the face from top to bottom. On one side, the cheek is full, the eye is alive, and the mouth is made of flesh. On the other, bone shows through: the cheekbone sinks in, the eye socket is a hollow, the nose an opening, and the teeth are visible without lips. Try a simple exercise: imagine covering one side with your hand and looking only at the other. Either half works on its own, like a complete portrait. But together they say something that neither says alone. That is the power of this piece.

It is so small that it could not have been used to cover anyone’s face, so it is thought to have been a ritual object, an offering or an amulet, rather than a disguise.

But it is not a solitary oddity. In Tlatilco, pieces with double faces abound: there are figurines with two heads, others with a single face and three eyes, others with two faces sharing one head. It seems that this village thought of the world in pairs: living and dead, above and below, man and woman, one and the other. And it makes sense: this was a society of farmers, and whoever plants seeds soon learns that the world works in cycles, from rain to drought, from planting to harvest, from life to death.

Why did death matter so much to a community of farmers? Because they had it before them every day. The dead lived beneath the floor of the house, and every harvest repeated the same cycle: the seed is buried, and thanks to that, the plant is born. For them, life did not replace death: it needed it.

That idea did not fade with time. The Mexica carried it into their myths, with Mictlantecuhtli, the lord of the dead, and they dressed it in sculpture: notice the skull at the center of the necklace of [Coatlicue](mna_s06_coatlicue), in the Mexica Hall. And it is still alive today: upstairs, in the hall of the Huastecs and the Totonacs, the [Xantolo altar](mna_s18_altar_xantolo) welcomes the dead each year, as they return to sit and eat with the living.

So, when you look at this little face, do not think of fear. Think of balance. And here is a fact that helps measure time: this little face is about two thousand years older than the [Sun Stone](mna_s06_piedra_sol). When the Mexica spoke of duality, they were taking up an idea that already had a very long history. Three thousand years ago, someone understood that life cannot be understood without death, and wrote it in clay, on a single face.

texto: Follow with your eyes the line that splits the face into two halves
Compare the eye on the living side with the empty socket on the skull side
Find the teeth without lips on the fleshless half

texto.Dimensions: 0.085 m tall x 0.073 m wide x 0.05 m thick

texto.pregunta: Myth: The split little face is a terror mask meant to frighten enemies.
texto.respuesta: Reality: It is a small ritual piece that expresses duality: life and death as two faces of a single cycle.
